title: India Says US Green Card Curbs 'Do Not Advance' Shared Ambitions
excerpt: The MEA slammed JD Vance's 'indentured servants' remark as deeply offensive and clarified that the PERM suspension will not touch existing H-1B visas — even as green card paths narrow.
body:
• India's Ministry of External Affairs said on Friday that the latest US restrictions on green card sponsorship "do not advance the shared ambitions" of India and the United States, urging recognition of the value of skilled migration.
  • New Delhi also called US Vice President JD Vance's description of H-1B workers as "indentured servants" deeply offensive, saying it ignored the contributions of Indian professionals to the American economy.
  • The MEA clarified that the suspension of PERM labour-certification processing is separate from the H-1B system and will not automatically affect existing visas — but it could complicate the green card path for affected employees.
  • If you or a family member are in the US green card queue through an employer, the immediate step is to check whether your employer's PERM filings are among the suspended ones; pending applications are frozen, not cancelled.

New Delhi pushes back

India on Friday issued its sharpest response yet to the Trump administration's widening crackdown on employment-based immigration, saying the latest US measures restricting green card sponsorship did not advance the shared ambitions of the two countries.

https://x.com/BRICSinfo/status/2108458349599871465

"The latest US measures did not advance the shared ambitions of the two countries," the Ministry of External Affairs said in a statement, according to Gulf News, urging all stakeholders to recognise the value of skilled migration. The ministry stressed that the movement of skilled workers benefits both nations — supporting research, productivity, competitiveness and job creation.

'Deeply offensive'

The statement also took aim at US Vice President JD Vance, who on Thursday described H-1B visa workers as "indentured servants" at a news conference. India called the remark deeply offensive and insensitive, given the term's historical and colonial associations.

"We believe that such descriptions are unwarranted and ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem."

— Ministry of External Affairs

Vance had accused foreign outsourcing companies of hiring overseas workers at lower salaries and replacing American employees to cut costs. He claimed H-1B visa holders earned $20,000 less than American citizens in similar positions, and that workers brought in by foreign outsourcing firms earned $48,000 less than Americans in comparable roles. "You bring in indentured servants from outside the country, you lay off American workers and, if you're a corporation, you make a ton of money by undercutting the wages of American workers," Vance said.

What the PERM suspension actually does

The MEA moved to clarify the technical scope of the US Department of Labor's decision to suspend processing of new and pending PERM (Permanent Labor Certification) applications for certain companies, including Microsoft, Adobe and major Indian IT providers such as TCS, Infosys, Wipro and HCL Technologies. The administration alleges misuse of the system and displacement of American workers.

Crucially, the ministry said the PERM suspension is separate from the H-1B visa system: it will not automatically affect existing H-1B visas or the legal status of visa holders and their dependants. The suspension does, however, threaten the green card process for eligible employees of the affected companies, because PERM is the mandatory first step before an employer can sponsor a worker for employment-based permanent residency.

Context: a year of tightening screws

The PERM freeze is the latest in a series of measures. In September 2025, the Trump administration announced a $100,000 fee for certain new H-1B visa applications, sending companies that depend on skilled foreign talent scrambling. A week ago, on October 8, the US suspended Microsoft, Adobe and six IT firms from the green card programme — a development The Videshi covered at the time.

Some analysts argue the crackdown could backfire. Former HCL Technologies CEO Vineet Nayar wrote on X that the restrictions may push more American technology work to India rather than protecting US jobs, the Economic Times reported. Nayar cited official figures showing 117,849 PERM certifications issued last year, of which Indian IT companies accounted for fewer than 1,400 — suggesting the direct exposure of Indian firms may be limited, but the signal on talent mobility is what matters.

What it means for Indian professionals in the US

For the hundreds of thousands of Indians working in the United States on H-1B visas — and their families — the MEA's statement is diplomatic cover, not legal relief. Workers employed by companies whose PERM applications are suspended face a frozen, not cancelled, green card pipeline: the practical effect is delay and uncertainty, particularly for those deep in multi-year adjustment-of-status queues.

Anyone affected should confirm with their employer's immigration counsel whether their PERM filing is among the suspended applications, and watch for whether the Department of Labor issues further guidance. The October visa bulletin restored EB-2 India movement, but administrative freezes operate independently of bulletin dates.

What's next

Watch for three things: whether US courts or Congress push back on the Department of Labor's suspension authority, whether the administration extends the freeze to more employers, and whether New Delhi escalates beyond statements — immigration has rarely figured this prominently in the bilateral relationship, and India's unusually blunt language suggests it is prepared to make it a negotiating issue.
